newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Indonesia, Malaysia looking for meal, trade quiet.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia, Malaysia looking for meal, trade quiet.

text.p: Indonesia and Malaysia are looking to buy up to 100,000 tonnes of soymeal for forward delivery while the rest of the region remains glued to the sidelines, grains and oilseeds traders said on Thursday.

"Indonesia is in the market for about 20,000 to 60,000 tonnes of soymeal for February/March. The Malaysians should be in for about 40,000 tonnes of meal for February/April. The question really is a matter of timing," a senior trader for a European commodity house told Reuters.
"The Malaysians have been snooping around for April. I think there's also some options for February/March, but time is on their side," a dealer in a U.S. commodity trading firm added.
Thailand may be looking for small cargoes of meal for forward delivery, but nothing larger than 10,000 tonnes.

The rest of the grains and oilseeds trade remained quiet after a rally in corn, wheat and soybean futures prices on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) bumped Southeast Asian buyers out of the market, traders said.
Buyers hoping for lower prices after release of the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) November crop report were disappointed when the CBOT headed in the opposite direction.
The December corn contract closed on Wednesday 4-3/4 U.S. cents up at US$2.70 a bushel. Regional buyers were hoping it would head towards $2.50 a bushel.

"We were just about ready to see some people jump in to buy. If prices had hung on, you could have seen some guys putting on a bit of insurance coverage. Now, the rest of Southeast Asia is absolutely dead," one trader said.
"Everyone is waiting for Christmas and hoping prices will come off. It's real quiet now," a U.S. trader said.
Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia are well-covered for corn and the only business which will probably be done may be some tenders in Taiwan or South Korea, dealers said.

"Corn is a dirty word in the region at the moment. Why should the buyers here go in and chase the prices? I don't believe there will be any substantial demand until possibly the end of December," one trader said.
Another dealer explained that most buyers may be mistaken waiting for prices to tumble lower.

"The evidence is gathering steam that prices may have bottomed out, but the buyers are not convinced about that," he said. "Everything is down as a result. Nobody is going to buy at these levels." Prices of grains and oilseeds rose across the board in tandem with firm CBOT prices, dealers said.

The price of U.S. corn coming into Southeast Asia was priced by regional dealers at around $150-$152 a tonne C&F on a Panamax vessel for January/February shipment against $148-$150 a tonne C&F last week.
U.S. soybeans edged up to around $308-$310 a tonne C&F for January/February shipment on a Panamax against $300-$307 a tonne C&F the previous week, the dealers said.
Indian-origin meal was quoted at about $310-$314 a tonne C&F for January/February shipment on a Tweendecker against $306-$308 a tonne C&F last week, they said.
U.S. low-protein soymeal prices jumped to about $305-$315 a tonne C&F for January/February on board a Panamax from $295-$297 a tonne C&F last week, traders said.
